de_da8a3a4d3a7f45b1050d3f6d.text: der Brief. Ich schreibe einen Brief.

en_2fbdb9e7380d345a36f733fb.text: Learn der Brief as one piece. Nouns start with a capital letter. Plural: die Briefe.

en_829e5b9aac23ffd35c842a3b.text: Add -e: Brief → Briefe. All plural nouns use die.

en_ea8de47176461c1fc651cfe0.text: Picture a letter wearing a big capital B. On its envelope is a tiny label: der. Open the envelope and find the letters i then e inside.

en_e5049f93e7e0ff4305104c57.text: ie, not ei. Capital B. Say the article with it: der Brief.

de_f4e20efd18c03c1d42562539.text: sich fühlen. Ich fühle mich gut.

en_cc508c0b8bd8624792891a4c.text: The ü matters. Change sich with the person: ich fühle mich, du fühlst dich, wir fühlen uns.

en_db5b5cd42b44eabb35d4cc27.text: With ich, use mich: Ich fühle mich gut.

en_b22c20d24dad9a2d4b613596.text: With du, use dich: Du fühlst dich müde.

en_aa883cc448fb1735031dece6.text: Picture a feelings thermometer. The two dots over ü are its two eyes, checking how you feel. Point at yourself when you say mich.

en_22a72c026210bcc7b8832eb4.text: ü has two dots; a silent h follows it. Keep sich with the infinitive.

de_dec382f029af28fa29beb8cd.text: sich ärgern. Ich ärgere mich über den Lärm.

de_57b88e658b54927c240c7b5c.text: Ich ärgere mich über den Lärm.

en_f372c2ae782dd75c56a07c7d.text: ärgern starts with ä. Learn the whole phrase: sich ärgern. Ich ärgere mich means I get annoyed.

de_4a43d41917db032b9a722ea9.text: Wir ärgern uns über den Regen.

en_9fe90c7781ee413d0fb0aea8.text: Ich pairs with mich. The extra e in ärgere belongs to the ich form.

en_16102671a4db964a66bd7463.text: Wir pairs with uns: Wir ärgern uns.

en_613ce0465d0193146bba2b85.text: Imagine the two dots over ä turning into annoyed eyebrows. A noisy alarm makes you point at yourself: Ich ärgere mich!

en_cbee67b8a832b8fbe8309fed.text: Start with ä, then r-g-ern. In ich ärgere, the ending changes to -e.

en_a9f033c308e30575c30c3366.text: Picture a sad face. Say trau-rig in two parts. It ends in -ig, not -ich.

en_e5aad1188e3efdc9bfab4091.text: Picture a sad face on a rainy window. Draw a tiny tear next to traurig. Pair it with the opposite: glücklich, happy.

en_61af535e5b7d8f254232f7da.text: Two chunks: trau + rig. Keep au together and end with g, not ch.

de_b0fd7459f0bed40c8386ca12.text: der Job. Mein Vater hat einen Job.

en_5f5281b0e904cfea87ae18c0.text: Same word as English, but German adds a capital J and der. Plural: die Jobs.

en_93da6cd3be08889da1a0a89d.text: Imagine a job badge with a giant J. The badge belongs to DER boss. The word already looks familiar from English.

en_bb18e7c6bdea9217c8b7ec57.text: Capital J, article der. Add s for the plural: Jobs.

en_83173cb3d69a921d43224195.text: mit + kommen = come along. In a simple statement, mit moves to the end: Ich komme mit.

en_242d6b13bf0a90fbc7d81594.text: Conjugate kommen → komme. Put mit at the end: Ich komme heute mit.

en_66db0f19055be07237d18df1.text: With wir, use kommen. The prefix mit goes at the end.

en_de455aae2ac0b62174334249.text: Your friend says “Come along!” Two m letters walk side by side. In a sentence, mit runs ahead to wait at the very end.

en_95eac26fd170d726591b4ae7.text: Two m letters in kommen. Join mitkommen in the infinitive; split komme … mit in a statement.

de_197790b9c224bd0e4453ef3b.text: umziehen. Wir ziehen nach Berlin um.

en_e5052ae0f31e08371934801f.text: Here umziehen means move home. Split it: ziehen … um. Keep ie together in ziehen.

en_95775e58b06ad75b255d5717.text: Wir ziehen morgen um. The prefix um goes at the end.

en_cd0c9a6bbb7bc1afb48a79cc.text: Ich needs ziehe. Keep um at the end.

en_85d9c5411c76d7835a04eca0.text: Imagine a moving box marked um. Inside, i and e stand in order next to a tall h. The box moves to the end: Wir ziehen um.

en_be1846f3b7f9186d9d1751d3.text: ie, then h. Infinitive umziehen is one word.

de_2b29a0de256663af639d1066.text: weit weg. Meine Freundin wohnt weit weg.

en_2e148f118fd800b1a3285d22.text: Two words: weit means far, weg means away. Remember the space.

en_c3db9b98950c7304049fdaea.text: Imagine two signposts far apart: WEIT on one, WEG on the other. The big gap reminds you to put a space between the words.

en_a81a3b7df5d3685ab3168507.text: Two words, both starting with w. First word has ei; second ends in g.

en_0fd768416e634cc2772408f2.text: False friend! German fast means almost. English fast would usually be schnell.

en_7ac7a15764c0db939cfda9d4.text: Imagine a race runner ALMOST at the finish. Freeze the picture just before the line. German fast means almost, even though English fast makes you think of speed.

en_aa3e761e13c80c1b97b28168.text: f-a-s-t. The spelling is familiar; the meaning is the trap.

de_da3983e47c9eaf4042d5273e.text: sich treffen. Wir treffen uns im Park.

en_7a678c757545211ae0626cea.text: Double f: treffen. For meeting each other, use uns with wir and euch with ihr.

en_811b2244b25c1a7c23c600fc.text: Wir treffen uns means we meet each other.

en_559940086f1b3ec5213dfb89.text: With ihr, use euch: Ihr trefft euch.

en_cc91423143bd428750a33db0.text: Picture the two f letters as two friends meeting in a park. They stand together in the middle of treffen.

en_9d4862dd75d4c7f358bf1a5b.text: Double f. Include sich in the vocabulary form; wir treffen uns in a sentence.

en_60dc98d2506f451b95168cd3.text: beide means exactly two. Keep ei in that order: b-e-i-d-e.

en_66bc3f262124579073735f6e.text: Hold up exactly two fingers. Both fingers stand over ei in beide. Both means two, not just some.

en_dbd05c82a767b15c2ccdfe35.text: ei, not ie. End with de.

de_d627ea0b6b2075ee813c9b6c.text: der Fahrradtrial. Der Fahrradtrial ist schwer.

en_ea54235c5f95860d35e5e13a.text: A bike trial is riding over obstacles. Build the spelling: Fahr + rad + trial. The two r letters meet in Fahrrad. Plural: die Fahrradtrials.

en_4aef472f6382548c17d390ef.text: In this lesson, use der Fahrradtrial and die Fahrradtrials.

en_09ada898319285a1e956cf7f.text: Learn the article supplied in your lesson: der Fahrradtrial.

en_672e248dbde3ddd10b499f03.text: Imagine a bike balancing over three blocks labeled Fahr, rad, trial. The r at the end of Fahr bumps into the r at the start of rad: rr.

en_798ddb9521123b6905e21b60.text: Capital F, two r letters at the join. Learn der Fahrradtrial. Finish trial, not trail.

de_8a2f5ada66e109ca5fa4b4c4.text: hochfahren. Ich fahre den Berg hoch.

en_307861a694b41e122694d24d.text: hoch means up; fahren means go by vehicle or ride. In a statement, split fahren … hoch.

en_473c3cbd7d310e14505a60fd.text: Ich fahre den Berg hoch. The prefix hoch goes at the end.

en_332636908196bec31b70a1d7.text: Er uses fährt, with ä. The prefix hoch goes at the end.

en_f0afe33919ad75e540f5e3a1.text: Imagine a bike going hoch (up) a hill. At the summit, hoch is waiting at the end of the sentence: Ich fahre den Berg hoch.

en_677910a906d56d5f98e247cf.text: hoch ends in ch; fahren contains h after a. Er fährt adds ä.

en_6559cc4b0ccc0b527390fd1f.text: Split it: hoffen + tlich. There are two f letters and a t before lich.

en_c375de5c0ce6f8449c5d6153.text: Imagine two fingers crossed for hope: ff. Beside them stands a tiny T-shaped sign pointing to lich. Hopefully your wish comes true.

en_0b11d3153e91947bc4c2a787.text: Double f AND the t: hoffen + t + lich.

de_41c9605861e3c7a6777e449d.text: die Treppe. Die Treppe ist hoch.

en_a5042676f4d693c0cdaef91a.text: Learn die Treppe. Double p, and a capital T. Plural: die Treppen.

en_7d473b02d5da5c0d8dbef071.text: Imagine the two p letters as two steps in a staircase. A sign at the bottom says die; a capital T stands at the top.

en_706f691bfee47f46b0fdbc23.text: Capital T and double p. Plural adds n: Treppen.

en_6aae151adcd476b9ef041c07.text: Picture someone lifting something heavy: stark = strong. Finish with rk.

en_ee198cd1a5130ff7db7829ff.text: Picture a strong person lifting the letters r and k like two heavy weights. The word ends with both weights: rk.

en_49ed9f59fa58cbcb2073b95a.text: st at the start, rk at the end. No extra vowel between r and k.

en_a3c09f6f53140c3290a94e78.text: Keep ei in streiten. The lesson uses streiten; wir streiten means we argue.

en_06e174c52d96571698987a1a.text: For ich, drop -n from streiten: ich streite.

en_d3db38430e9a00b82ff47644.text: The er form is streitet. The extra e makes the ending pronounceable.

en_4ecadbb11186c9a43a6ef196.text: Imagine two friends arguing over who goes first: e or i. Settle it: e goes before i in streiten.

en_ba57fe5c87d19a05a15e98d1.text: Start str; use ei, not ie. The ending is -ten.

en_79b9336b6b5d827f58dbfea4.text: The two dots matter: müde, not mude. Think of feeling tired after a long school day.

de_756ae781803ae9fe81d1f59c.text: Nach der Schule sind wir müde.

en_707e4b63e111dee06de40389.text: Picture a tired face. The two dots over ü are sleepy eyes. Put the eyes back before you let the word go to bed.

en_5ecb3d50859040c02ea703a5.text: Four letters: m-ü-d-e. The umlaut is part of the letter.

en_4a7bbe4d0f8d7010bab50b57.text: Build it: sch + lecht. Watch the ch before the final t.

en_bea5b214c3d1d4feea780b39.text: Imagine a BAD weather report. Rain falls on a sign split into four pieces: sch / le / ch / t. Rebuild it before the storm arrives.

en_c872615aba12bfa1ab48ecda.text: There is ch inside sch at the start, and another ch before the last t.

en_814b1cc98ca811baea955bbe.text: ver + liebt. Keep ie, then bt. With sein: Ich bin verliebt.

en_f7fbdaecb8db00f66e93c01d.text: Picture a love note folded around ie. A little b and t seal the end of the note together.

en_64a56fc98e156715af0ef831.text: ie, not ei. Finish with bt, not pt.

en_9dce62aa19ebe506f9487d77.text: In this lesson, bestimmt means definitely. Double m: be-stimmt.

en_9698f2f3054b045cb33556f2.text: Imagine a big DEFINITELY stamp. Two m-shaped stamp handles press down together, with a final t as the stamp’s handle.

en_28e8e90e35360d7a14f42758.text: Double m, then t. The whole ending is -immt.

en_da87c084f00bfb732d499df0.text: Build Glück + lich. Keep ü and ck. glücklich is happy; traurig is sad.

en_abec2d81df07ec9c3acc69a4.text: Glück means luck or happiness. Imagine finding a lucky coin and smiling: glücklich. The two dots over ü are your happy eyes.

en_dbb860011ec256b35fe5dbf5.text: ü + ck, then lich. There is no extra k after lich.

en_3b3588ca6a8d78bff85d610e.text: Another false friend: sensibel means sensitive, not sensible. It ends in -bel.

en_04fb2d79196db41dcd26c231.text: Picture a sensitive person noticing a tiny sound from a bell. Let that bell remind you of the ending -bel, with only one l.

en_525cd5c44b548ec236667897.text: sen-si-bel, not the English word sensible. Meaning: sensitive.

en_45b62b1f83fee9474491e699.text: Keep ei and ß: fl-ei-ß-ig. Use the ß key below the answer box.

en_0f7f41b18a1c7b06193004d9.text: Imagine a hard-working student carefully writing ei and then a big ß on a checklist. Every detail gets checked.

en_8e1656c33540a6f71af03348.text: ei, then ß, then ig. For this German lesson use ß, even though Swiss spelling uses ss.

en_2efddd4746a38b5d523093d1.text: zu + hören. The ö matters. In a statement: Ich höre dir zu. Listening to someone uses dative, here dir.

en_f5ed62f6e127055577230e2e.text: Ich höre dir zu. Keep ö in höre and put zu at the end.

en_4e1710677d516fc3ba8b6f68.text: Wir hören dir zu. The prefix zu goes at the end.

en_4ee19975465efe2631036998.text: Imagine the dots over ö as two ears listening. The word zu walks to the end while those ears listen: Ich höre dir zu.

en_4f8b691af7122b07949781b1.text: ö, not o. Join zuhören in the infinitive; split höre … zu in a statement.

en_914f37a9770f2214ff46aea5.text: einige means some or several. It does not mean exactly two; that is beide.

en_303894113a10fee1317f5624.text: Imagine a basket with some apples. Label three parts of the basket ei / ni / ge. There are several apples, not exactly two.

en_dbb7cdfa288b56105e37621d.text: Start ei, not ie. Three chunks: ei-ni-ge.

de_7bd90e032f0bf41b15378552.text: sich interessieren. Ich interessiere mich für Musik.

en_efec752148908332d993ecf5.text: One r, double s: inter-ess-ieren. Use sich interessieren für, with mich for ich.

en_2f92489fc0cf3b4c2b2b6b3a.text: Ich pairs with mich. Für means in in this expression.

en_14dd62f0d0e2aa363d2c8c7c.text: Wir pairs with uns: Wir interessieren uns für Sport.

en_dba6b9ed7bec749fd109f6f3.text: Imagine an interesting museum. One r guards the entrance in inter; two s letters are the exhibits in ess. Follow the signs: inter / ess / ier / en.

en_675056b0de10c179f5f058c8.text: inter has one r. ess has two s letters. Keep ie in -ieren. Include sich.

en_62edb760f20ad9acf4c5878d.text: A brief message can go in a letter. English brief and German Brief share the same letters, but der Brief means the letter itself.

en_3b8d7d12331ce0447228e46e.text: Learn der Brief together. Capital B; ie, not ei. More than one: die Briefe.

en_1f4b31f7f952ce971e96916e.text: Before a match, check how you feel: Ich fühle mich gut — I feel good. The feeling is about you, so keep the ‘myself’ part: mich.

en_f43382fc27fd9df4021ab937.text: sich fühlen: ü, then h. Keep sich when learning the verb; use mich with ich.

en_4bc75cddb9f07649cdf61bbe.text: Someone's loud video interrupts your homework. Ich ärgere mich über den Lärm. Ärger means annoyance or trouble; here you are getting annoyed by the noise.

en_7f6622af7c8494cb9b93f204.text: Write sich ärgern: initial ä, then rgern. Ich uses ärgere mich; wir uses ärgern uns.

en_580e74dc647d499e80f5df87.text: Your friend moves away: traurig means sad. It’s a feeling, not tiredness. Learn the word in two short spelling blocks: trau + rig.

en_c22dec91342595e0dc8aa10b.text: Keep au together. End with rig: the final written letter is g, even if it sounds different.

en_e9b380403ac03010e0f1d268.text: Easy transfer: a job is der Job. You already know the English spelling; the new information is the German article and capital letter.

en_e2e1e660e9c4f42c2de9dc8e.text: der Job: capital J. Plural die Jobs adds s, just like English.

en_90fddfc3b6db0da34f948f30.text: Friends head to the park and invite you along. Mit means with; kommen means come. Ich komme mit. Picture joining their group at the door.

en_d9b92d8bfdcb649841a765ae.text: Write mitkommen as one infinitive, with double m in kommen. In Ich komme mit, mit moves to the end.

en_24ea22b66315d3f36d3c6f08.text: Think moving house, not walking across the room: Wir ziehen um — We’re moving. Keep the moving verb as one word when naming it: umziehen.

en_ecee23dd5b43c295e179c6fb.text: um + ziehen. In ziehen, write ie followed by h. In Wir ziehen um, um goes last.

en_d27e0916341b3b0c2dd49d2a.text: Your base is far away on the map: weit weg. Two separate words, two w starts. The space is part of the answer.

en_f203ef8c4c3b6405837b2b8d.text: weit has ei; weg ends in g. Keep a space between them.

en_4b8aaef1d81350f8ba6d971d.text: Your download is at 99%: fast fertig — almost finished. German fast means almost, not speedy. Think nearly done, not going quickly.

en_ed647c6d0d889502dab15e48.text: Same letters as English fast; different meaning. Write f-a-s-t, with no extra letters.

en_7577fe1b60edcd7058f5dcf6.text: Meet your friend at spawn: Wir treffen uns — We meet up. The two f letters make a simple pair to remember: two friends meeting.

en_c66ae92ee6244fa79d587827.text: sich treffen: double f, one t at the start. Learn sich too; wir takes uns.

en_70a9ae7eb7502ccb0d954278.text: Two players, and both are ready: beide. Both means exactly two; don’t mix it up with einige, which means some or several.

en_47d6fdb53a992818dc0472d4.text: b + ei + de. The vowel pair is ei, not ie; finish with e.

en_88e910f898ccc2b3fc06c749.text: Bike trials means balancing a bike over obstacles, not riding a trail. Build the name from Fahr + rad + trial; the r letters meet at the join.

en_63d410f7c851f711ccdab866.text: Your class sheet uses der Fahrradtrial. Keep capital F, the rr join, and trial with i before a.

en_978c4cbb887c5677d9e9c9bf.text: Ride up a hill: hoch means up, fahren means travel by vehicle. Together: hochfahren. In Ich fahre hoch, the up part moves to the end.

en_7934cbe7789327efb2c3e761.text: hoch + fahren. Keep ch in hoch and the h after a in fahren.

en_957543a62a739ac7aad28da6.text: Before opening a chest: Hoffentlich! — Hopefully! Link it to hoffen, meaning to hope. For spelling, build hoffen + t + lich; don’t lose that linking t.

en_6265833a3ab8858ca0e5f1b6.text: Double f, then the t before lich. End with ch, not ck.

en_0335770c22527444bdb56777.text: At school, you take the staircase to the next floor: Ich gehe die Treppe hoch. Picture the actual steps you use each day.

en_8d0eaf9a099ca0d8668bb4ad.text: Write die Treppe with capital T, double p, and final e. Plural: die Treppen.

en_9135e671e649b7a3c6b92b44.text: Tony Stark has a strong suit. Use Stark as a name hook for stark — strong. The German adjective stays lowercase; this is a memory link, not a translation rule.

en_408476e350f2bcf15098508b.text: st + ark. Finish rk, with no vowel between r and k. Lowercase s.

en_dfe0493300d4f556a6331246.text: Two teammates argue about the plan: Sie streiten — They argue. This is the argument itself; sich ärgern is feeling annoyed.

en_14560d225638387d079b7d20.text: str + ei + ten. Three consonants at the start; ei, not ie.

en_ee2d6f958eab9b6c2d32d3e5.text: After a late gaming session: Ich bin müde — I’m tired. Keep it separate from traurig: you need sleep, not cheering up.

en_b4273e44c45a237657394564.text: m + ü + de. The two dots belong to ü; plain u is a different letter.

en_32df8483549cc86d623fdfd4.text: A bad connection makes the game lag: schlecht means bad. Build its spelling in four blocks: sch / le / ch / t.

en_a521e4ccc7266bbac350ff94.text: Start sch. There is another ch before the final t; don’t drop that second h.

en_19505a7d53651e7d51e95259.text: Liebe means love; verliebt means in love. The shared lieb gives you the meaning and the tricky ie spelling in one useful link.

en_1841e6707b8ef2751d36c8ed.text: ver + lieb + t. Keep ie together; finish bt, not pt.

en_3ffed8b1178fb4282d7f2c35.text: ‘Will you join us?’ ‘Definitely!’ That confident answer is bestimmt in this lesson. It’s a yes with confidence, not just a hopeful maybe.

en_d2ef26deb03922ffe35859e3.text: be + stimmt. Double m followed by t; don’t shorten the ending to one m.

en_ea21a543d866fd9332511c66.text: Glück means luck or happiness. Finding diamonds can make you glücklich — happy. The useful spelling link is Glück + lich, with a lowercase start for the adjective.

en_70f83d8bd9691d50c8abea44.text: glücklich: lowercase g, ü, ck, then lich. The ending is ch, not ck.

en_c8ddd4a8a798d213177e77ab.text: A friend notices when someone's joke hurts another person. Mein Freund ist sensibel. The shared sensi in sensitive and sensibel anchors the meaning: sensitive.

en_e253175f93b7d011eae01dd3.text: Write sensibel with ending bel, not ble. It means sensitive, not the English sensible.

en_cb49a2dfa275d85b5c761c61.text: A classmate steadily researches, writes, and improves a project. Sie ist fleißig. Fleiß means diligence; the adjective describes the person putting in that work.

en_749d002b32e2db22957967c3.text: Write fleißig with ei, ß, and final ig. Keep the lesson's ß spelling.

en_e8a4073d366b7dac650e70ac.text: A friend explains something important, and you put your phone down. Ich höre dir zu. Hören means hear; the added zu marks listening attentively to someone.

en_e30fdef305a148407d98a049.text: Write zuhören with ö. In Ich höre dir zu, zu goes last; dir is the dative form for you.

en_ac0d82ce19e6529f47257db3.text: You have some blocks left, not necessarily two: einige. Contrast beide, meaning both of two. Spell it in three small blocks: ei + ni + ge.

en_02cf4e2ab8398a5bf70e5486.text: Start ei, not ie. Keep the middle i: ei-ni-ge ends in e.

en_805d37344b8144f40b120033.text: Think of an interest you actually have: games, music, or sports. sich interessieren means to be interested. Use four spelling blocks: inter / ess / ier / en.

en_7eadba3452ee433916d62742.text: One r in inter; double s in ess; ie in ier. Include sich when naming the verb.

en_e4968ddd7880eeb6588850fa.text: Learn der Brief → die Briefe. In Ich schreibe einen Brief, einen means a: Brief receives the action, so masculine ein changes to einen. Brief keeps its capital B. Its long ee sound is written ie.

en_8eeeab6b3c069631e842c0bf.text: One letter: der Brief. Several letters: die Briefe. Add -e. Use die for the plural in this naming exercise; articles can change in other sentence roles.

en_189d9aaf4a8dcdb7f8d73352.text: English says I feel good. German says Ich fühle mich gut: it needs mich here, although English does not say myself. Match ich → mich, du → dich, wir → uns. For ü, try saying ee with rounded lips, then listen and copy the German sound. Keep the h after ü.

en_62bc4f8b7d136a846af9cb19.text: Before a match: Ich fühle mich gut — I feel good. German needs mich here, even though English does not say myself. Learn the whole phrase together.

en_63c343c316acb6a0ed718873.text: Learn sich ärgern über …: to get annoyed about something. Ich ärgere mich means I get annoyed; wir ärgern uns means we get annoyed. English leaves out myself/ourselves here, but German needs mich/uns. Start ärgern with ä.

en_63b3ea06f714139e8f27692d.text: Ich bin traurig means I am sad. Spell trau + rig. The au sounds like ow in cow. Listen to the German ending: even when it sounds like ich, write ig. Traurig is sad; müde is tired.

en_ba539019711eed305d035941.text: Learn der Job → die Jobs: the plural adds s. German nouns need a capital. In Mein Vater hat einen Job, einen means a; masculine ein changes to einen for the thing someone has.

en_24a0d958f90d61cdeccc27dc.text: mitkommen means come along. Learn Ich komme mit — I am coming along. Change the verb for the person: du kommst, wir kommen. In these simple statements, keep mit at the end. The dictionary form mitkommen is one word, with double m.

en_ae2f549557e5385391fe49fd.text: Here umziehen means move home, not walk across a room. Ich ziehe um — I am moving. Wir ziehen um — We are moving. In these statements um goes last. In ziehen, ie makes a long ee sound and is followed by a silent h.

en_b639497fab9198671ab97aca.text: weit means far; weg means away. Keep two words: weit weg. In weit, ei sounds like English eye. Hear the final sound in weg, but remember the written ending is g.

en_e344dada46f36568854edf4b.text: beide means both of two: Wir sind beide müde — We are both tired. In beide, ei sounds like English eye. Contrast einige: some or several, without specifying exactly two.

en_dfd87f1f0aa4be93f65f97a9.text: Bike trials involves balancing and riding over obstacles, not following a trail. Build Fahr + rad + trial; the r letters meet. Your class sheet uses der Fahrradtrial → die Fahrradtrials. The sporting word Trial is normally das Trial; ask your teacher about this article difference. These exercises follow the sheet.

en_5c97dbae5f4843e82e17b82d.text: hochfahren means ride or drive up. Compare Ich fahre hoch — I ride up; Er fährt hoch — He rides up. With er, a changes to ä; wir keeps fahren. In these simple statements hoch goes at the end. Keep the silent h in fahren.

en_62f2c5c7ff359035ce94c1c9.text: Compare ich fahre and er fährt: with er, a changes to ä and the ending is t. Er fährt den Berg hoch — He rides up the mountain. Put hoch at the end.

en_3231361d3a3e30b2a8179d30.text: die Treppe means one staircase. English often calls this the stairs, but German Treppe is singular. Multiple staircases: die Treppen. Keep capital T and double p. Ich gehe die Treppe hoch means I am going up the stairs.

en_525d1564dcbcce0790cecc86.text: One staircase: die Treppe. Several staircases: die Treppen. Add n. English the stairs can describe just one German Treppe.

en_a4b8ad8c17080a69837e00dc.text: die Treppe is one staircase, often called the stairs in English. Several staircases: die Treppen. Keep capital T, double p, and final e in Treppe.

en_8f9b0a7c2b6a5c92b9e25317.text: streiten means argue: wir streiten — we argue. Use ich streite, but er streitet: the extra e before t helps you say the ending. The ei sounds like English eye. Arguing is an action; sich ärgern means feeling annoyed.

en_c4d796790ad6c9dd33f80016.text: Ich bin müde — I am tired. For ü, try ee with rounded lips, then listen and copy the German sound. Keep the dots: u is a different vowel. Spell mü + de. Needing sleep is müde, not traurig (sad).

en_60d28290a3465a8a9f108504.text: schlecht means bad. Build sch + le + ch + t. The first sch sounds like English sh; the later ch is a different German sound, not English ch in chair. Listen and copy. Keep both h letters.

en_492ed1a7736e41d6d43e30ba.text: Liebe means love. Build ver + lieb + t: verliebt means in love. Ich bin verliebt — I am in love. The ie sounds like ee; keep written bt even when the b sounds like p.

en_397d1b3a37a60aefccf06b6c.text: Ich bin glücklich — I am happy. Build Glück + lich, then use a lowercase g for the adjective. Keep ü, ck, and the different ending ch. Compare glücklich (happy) and traurig (sad). Listen to ü and ch before repeating.

en_d59fe58d9058f93447731d3e.text: fleißig means hard-working: Sie ist fleißig — She works hard. Build fleiß + ig. The ei sounds like English eye; ß sounds like s, not b. Keep the written ending ig. Use the ß key below the answer box.

en_259b70b55353edee7af8af2b.text: Your friend keeps working on a build, even when it takes a few tries. Sie ist fleißig — She is hard-working. Think steady effort, not finishing fast.

en_90b0213c0ee9cffa46a11b29.text: fleiß + ig: ei sounds like eye; ß sounds like s, not b. Keep the written ending ig and use the ß button.

en_f52394138be2073565e54e7a.text: Learn Ich höre dir zu — I am listening to you. German uses dir, not dich, with zuhören: learn höre dir zu as a phrase. Wir hören dir zu — We are listening to you. In these simple statements zu goes last. Listen to ö; it is not the same sound as o.

en_e53ae8c963a4174598a816f1.text: Write zuhören with ö. Learn höre dir zu as a phrase: listening to you. German uses dir here, not dich. In Ich höre dir zu, zu goes last.

en_bbe5e6bffa197f32d988a2f3.text: There are two r letters, neither doubled: one in inter and another in ieren. Keep double s: inter + ess + ieren. Learn Ich interessiere mich für Musik — I am interested in music. German needs mich and für here; do not translate English in word for word.

en_f99ba9a696f1c46e51a02241.text: Two r letters, neither doubled: one in inter, another in ier. Double s; ie in ier. Learn sich interessieren für: to be interested in.
